kurz: How, within eleven years, first the dollar's link to gold ended, then the oil price rose, and in the end a recession was needed to bring inflation expectations back down.

bloecke.md:
On 15 August 1971, Richard Nixon ended the post-war monetary system with a television address. After three days of closed-door talks at Camp David, he suspended the obligation to convert foreign central banks' dollars into gold at a rate of $35 per fine ounce. With the Smithsonian Agreement of December 1971, the parity was devalued to $38. The agreement lasted less than two years, and in March 1973 the major currencies moved to floating exchange rates.

The end of gold convertibility removed more than a technical rule. Until then, every government had been subject to a limit set from outside, because a country that created too much money lost gold. After that, only a domestic political decision limited money creation. The eleven years up to 1982 show what happens when this decision goes wrong, and what the correction costs.

## Inflation before the first oil crisis

OPEC is often blamed for the inflation of the 1970s. But inflation began earlier. In the USA, it rose from 1.6% (1965) through 4.3% (1968) to 5.8% (1970), that is, years before the first embargo. In West Germany, it stood at 5.2% in 1971 and 5.4% in 1972, after having mostly remained below 3% throughout the previous decade.

The causes lay in the countries' own economic policies. The USA financed the Vietnam War and social programmes at the same time without raising taxes accordingly. The Fed under Arthur Burns kept interest rates too low out of consideration for employment and election dates. This pattern later became known as stop-go. The central bank tightened monetary policy until unemployment rose, and loosened it again before inflation had been broken. Surplus countries such as West Germany imported part of this inflation because until 1973 they had to buy up incoming dollars at the fixed rate. The oil price shock therefore hit a market that was already overheated.

bloecke.titel: Inflation rates in Germany and the USA, 1965 to 1985
bloecke.unter: In both countries, the rise begins before 1973. The oil crises reinforced a trend that they had not triggered.

bloecke.md:
## Two supply shocks

On 17 October 1973, eleven days after the start of the Yom Kippur War, OAPEC decided on production cuts and a supply embargo against states that supported Israel. The price of crude oil rose from around $3 per barrel to over $5, and the following year to just under $12. West Germany responded with four car-free Sundays from 25 November 1973 and with a temporary speed limit of 100 kilometres per hour on motorways, which applied from November 1973 to March 1974. In 1974, it spent just under 23 billion Deutsche Marks on oil, almost 153% or around 14 billion Deutsche Marks more than in the previous year. This purchasing power flowed abroad without anything being created for it at home. In the second oil crisis, following the Iranian revolution, the price peaked at around $38 in 1980.

bloecke.titel: Crude oil price over the course of both oil crises
bloecke.unter: The price of crude oil, industry's most important input, rose twelvefold in seven years.

bloecke.md: A demand boom raises prices and output together. A higher interest rate counteracts this and costs only growth that was overheated anyway. In a supply shock, by contrast, prices rise while output falls. A rate rise then deepens the recession, and a rate cut entrenches inflation. The British politician Iain Macleod coined the word **stagflation** for this situation as early as 1965. The Phillips curve assumed a stable trade-off between unemployment and inflation. This assumption did not survive the decade, because in the end both were high at the same time.

## Consequences for investors

Between 11 January 1973 and 3 October 1974, the S&P 500 lost a total of 48.2%. In nominal terms, it did not regain its old level until 17 July 1980, around 90 months after the peak. This was the longest recovery time of the post-war period. After the dotcom crash, the index needed around 86 months, from March 2000 to May 2007. However, the nominal recovery concealed a large real loss.

Based on the annual rates of the US consumer price index CPI-U, the price level rose cumulatively by around 73% from 1973 to 1979.

`1.062 × 1.111 × 1.091 × 1.057 × 1.065 × 1.076 × 1.113 ≈ 1.735`

These rates compare annual averages. Based on the monthly values, the index rose from 42.6 points in January 1973 to 82.7 points in July 1980, that is, by around 94%. A dollar from the start of 1973 was therefore worth only about 52 cents in July 1980 (`1 ÷ 1.94`). In nominal terms, the portfolio was back at its starting point, but in real terms around 48% was missing. Dividends are not taken into account here; they made up part of this. The shares had regained their nominal value; the loss arose from the reduced purchasing power of the dollar in which they are measured.

bloecke.titel: Purchasing power of the dollar and the Deutsche Mark, annual average 1972 = 100
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation from the official annual inflation rates. By 1982, the dollar had lost around 57% of its purchasing power, the Deutsche Mark around 40%.

bloecke.md:
## The Volcker shock

Paul Volcker became Chairman of the Federal Reserve in August 1979. On 6 October 1979, he changed the monetary policy procedure. Instead of setting an interest rate, the Fed now steered the growth of bank reserves and left the overnight rate to the market. This rate rose sharply, and key interest rates at times reached around 20% in 1981. This fed through fully to the capital market. Ten-year US Treasury bonds yielded an annual average of 13.91% in 1981, the highest value in the entire series since 1954. Ten-year Bunds reached 10.13% in the same year, after 10.44% in the crisis year of 1974.

The result was a severe recession with double-digit unemployment and a wave of bankruptcies in the interest-sensitive construction and farming sectors. In protest, builders sent lengths of timber to the Fed. The tightening brought inflation down significantly: in the USA, it fell from 13.5% (1980) through 10.3% and 6.1% to 3.2% in 1983.

On the stock market, this second bear market was much milder. Between 28 November 1980 and 12 August 1982, prices fell by 27.1%. By 3 November 1982, the old level had already been regained, 705 days after the peak and just under three months after the low. This marked the start of the bull market that lasted until 2000. Prices therefore fell mainly while inflation was building up. They recovered when inflation was being fought credibly, even though this meant high interest rates and a recession.

bloecke.md:
## The milder course in Germany

The highest German inflation rates were 7.1% (1973) and 6.9% (1974). The 1974 figure was just over half the American figure of 11.1% in the same year. There are three reasons for this.

First, under Section 12 of the Bundesbank Act (Bundesbankgesetz), the Bundesbank was independent of instructions from the federal government, and it used this independence in 1973 against political resistance. Second, in 1974 it became the first major central bank to adopt a publicly announced money supply target, a forerunner of today's inflation targets. Third, the Deutsche Mark appreciated after the end of fixed exchange rates, which dampened the dollar-invoiced oil price in Deutsche Mark terms. The memory of the 1923 hyperinflation also gave the Bundesbank additional political backing.

## Taxation of nominal returns

For German investors, inflation has a second effect that is often overlooked, because the tax authorities tax nominal returns. In income tax law, Section 20 EStG (Income Tax Act) makes no deduction for inflation. Under Section 32d(1) EStG, capital income is subject to the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) of 25% plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge on that tax, 26.375% in total. Church tax may be added. Under Section 20(9) EStG, the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) is €1,000, or €2,000 for joint assessment. For equity funds, the 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) under Section 20(1) sentence 1 InvStG (Investment Tax Act) reduces the tax base. There is no such relief for interest income from instant-access savings accounts or bonds.

The higher inflation is, therefore, the larger the share of the tax that falls on purely illusory gains, that is, on returns that merely offset the loss of purchasing power. The following table shows three cases with practically the same real pre-tax return that turn out completely differently after tax.

bloecke.md: In September 2026, the ECB deposit facility rate is 2.50%, and the German inflation rate in August was 2.9%. An instant-access savings account paying 2.5% yields 1.84% after flat-rate withholding tax, so around minus 1.0% in real terms. High interest rates and high inflation almost always occur together. But only the interest rate is advertised, not the inflation rate. A savings product can therefore only be assessed if you calculate both figures together and after tax.

## Comparison with 2022 and today

In 2022, German annual inflation reached 6.9%, the same figure as in 1974. This time, too, an energy price shock came first. As back then, central banks tightened faster than in the decades in between, and shares and bonds fell at the same time because both depend on the same interest rate.

Today's situation differs in three respects. Long-term inflation expectations remained anchored at around 2% and did not rise into the high single digits. The independence of the central bank is enshrined in treaty law in the euro area under Article 130 TFEU (Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union), as is the prohibition of monetary financing of governments under Article 123 TFEU. In addition, wages in Germany are not automatically linked to a price index; second-round effects arise here only through collective wage bargaining.

In September 2026, the topic remains current. The German inflation rate was 2.9% in August, and the core rate excluding energy and food was 2.4%. Following tensions in the Middle East, it was above all the prices of energy (up 10.5%) and fuel (up 27.7%) that rose. On 10 September, the ECB raised all three key interest rates by 25 basis points, and the deposit facility rate has stood at 2.50% since 16 September. On 16 September, the Fed unanimously raised its key interest rate to 3.75-4.00%. Ten-year Bunds are yielding around 3.5%, as high as they last were in 2011. The 1970s are therefore not repeating themselves, but the basic pattern is the same, only an order of magnitude smaller.

Persistent inflation arises from expectations and not solely from a higher oil price. A supply shock raises the price level once. It only turns into lasting inflation when wages, prices and interest rates adjust in anticipation of a repetition. That is why, since 1982, central banks have aligned their policy with inflation expectations and not with the rate measured at any given time. Credibility is therefore a central bank's most important tool. Once it has lost its credibility, it can only regain it through a recession.

- Returns should be calculated in real terms and after tax. The nominal interest rate is the least important of the three figures.
- The price level and the inflation rate need to be considered separately. After the inflation wave of 2021 to 2023, the German price level is permanently above that of 2020, by just over a quarter in September 2026, and a falling rate does nothing to reverse this.
- Tangible assets protect against inflation in the long term, but not in the short term. In the 1973/74 shock, shares fell the most; the protection only became apparent in the years that followed.
- For bonds, [[Duration|duration]] determines interest rate risk. The price change is roughly minus duration times the change in interest rates, which is why long maturities multiplied the losses in 1974 and 1981. Inflation-linked German federal securities have not been newly issued since the end of 2023.

In the 1970s, many investors sought protection against inflation in precious metals, and that is where the next speculative bubble formed. The gold price rose from the abolished parity of $35 to around $850 by early 1980.

In silver, the Hunt brothers deliberately drove the price up. At the end of 1979, their companies controlled around 195 million fine ounces. The price rose from under $10 (mid-1979) to $34.45 on 31 December 1979 and to over $50 in January 1980. In response, the COMEX derivatives exchange imposed position limits and on 21 January restricted trading to closing out, that is, to closing existing positions. On Silver Thursday, 27 March 1980, the price fell to $10.80.

Two lessons follow from this. You cannot corner a market against the body that sets its rules. In addition, the protection against inflation was at times riskier than the inflation it was supposed to protect against.

mitnehmen: Since the Nixon shock of 15 August 1971, the international monetary system has had no external limit; only a political decision still limits money creation.
The inflation of the 1970s began before the first oil crisis, which reinforced the trend but did not trigger it.
A nominal recovery says nothing about real value: when the S&P 500 regained its 1973 level in July 1980, the dollar was worth around 48% less.
Volcker brought inflation down with interest rates of around 20% and a recession, and the stock market recovered as soon as the fight against inflation was credible.
The German tax authorities tax nominal returns without any deduction for inflation, so when inflation is high, a positive real return before tax can easily turn into a negative one after tax.

begriffe.text: Simultaneous occurrence of high inflation and weak or shrinking economic output. Stagflation is a typical consequence of a supply shock, against which monetary policy has no tool that solves both problems at once.

Sudden increase in the price or scarcity of an input, such as energy. A supply shock raises the price level and at the same time lowers output. A demand shock, by contrast, moves both in the same direction.

Suspension of the US dollar's convertibility into gold on 15 August 1971. This effectively marked the start of the pure fiat money system without gold backing, with predominantly floating exchange rates.
Passing on of a one-off price shock to wages and other prices. Only this turns a one-off shift in the price level into lasting inflation.

Nominal interest rate minus expected inflation (Fisher equation i = r + πᵉ). For savers, the real interest rate is the only meaningful figure, although the tax on the nominal return also has to be deducted.
